items.followUp: Define molecular formula and explain how it differs from an empirical formula.

rubric.why: The definition must identify that an empirical formula gives the simplest ratio of atoms or elements.
rubric.description: Defines the empirical formula as the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms of each element in a compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition conveying the simplest whole-number ratio.

rubric.why: A method for obtaining the formula is required.
rubric.description: Explains that it is determined from composition by converting amounts to moles and reducing the mole ratio to the simplest whole numbers.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid determination method, such as converting to moles and simplifying the ratio.

modelAnswer: An empirical formula represents the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound.
It is determined from the composition by converting the amounts of the elements to moles and reducing their mole ratio to the simplest whole numbers.

items.followUp: What substances and processes are studied in biochemistry? Give two examples.

rubric.why: The answer must identify biochemistry as chemistry applied to living organisms.
rubric.description: States that biochemistry is the study of the chemistry or chemical substances of living organisms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking chemical study with living organisms.

rubric.why: The scope includes chemical processes or substances found in living organisms.
rubric.description: Mentions a relevant process or subject within the field, such as metabolism, enzymes, proteins, or nucleic acids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming a relevant biochemical process or subject.

modelAnswer: Biochemistry is the branch of chemistry that studies the chemical substances and processes of living organisms.
Its scope includes biochemical processes such as metabolism and the study of substances such as enzymes, proteins and nucleic acids.

items.followUp: State two properties of cathode rays and explain how one property shows their nature.

rubric.why: Any one correct property earns credit.
rubric.description: Gives one valid property of cathode rays.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct property, such as straight-line travel, negative charge, or deflection by electric or magnetic fields.

rubric.why: A second distinct property is needed.
rubric.description: Gives a second valid property of cathode rays.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second correct property; do not award twice for repeating the same property.

modelAnswer: Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
They carry a negative charge and are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.

items.followUp: State one similarity and two differences between Rutherford’s and Bohr’s atomic models.

rubric.why: A comparison should establish the shared nuclear structure or identify the particles and their arrangement.
rubric.description: States a relevant point of comparison, such as electrons moving around a central, positively charged nucleus.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct structural comparison involving the nucleus and electrons.

rubric.why: The main distinction is that Bohr introduced fixed, quantized energy levels, unlike Rutherford’s model.
rubric.description: Identifies the difference between Rutherford’s and Bohr’s treatment of electron orbits or energy.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that Bohr proposed fixed energy levels or stationary orbits, while Rutherford did not.

modelAnswer: In both models, electrons move around a small, positively charged nucleus.
Rutherford’s model did not specify fixed electron energy levels, whereas Bohr proposed fixed orbits with definite, quantized energies.

items.followUp: Write the names of the elements in Group 2 and Period 3 of the Periodic Table.

rubric.why: The response should name the elements belonging to Group 1.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for listing Group 1 elements correctly; accept symbols in place of names.

rubric.why: The response should name the elements belonging to Period 2.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for listing Period 2 elements correctly; accept symbols in place of names.

modelAnswer: The Group 1 elements are hydrogen, lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium.
The Period 2 elements are lithium, beryllium, boron, carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, fluorine and neon.

items.followUp: Define electron affinity and write an equation showing the electron affinity of chlorine.

rubric.why: The definition must describe energy released when an atom accepts an electron.
rubric.description: Defines electron affinity as the energy released when a gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition including electron acceptance and energy release.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates electron acceptance by an atom.
rubric.description: Gives chlorine accepting an electron to form a chloride ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the chlorine example or its correctly written reaction.

modelAnswer: Electron affinity is the energy released when a neutral gaseous atom accepts an electron to form a negative ion.
For example: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g) + energy.

items.followUp: Describe the trend in ionisation energy across a period and down a group.

rubric.why: Atomic radius decreases across a period from left to right.
rubric.description: States that atomic radius generally decreases across a period from left to right.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction across a period.

rubric.why: Atomic radius increases down a group as additional electron shells are added.
rubric.description: States that atomic radius generally increases down a group.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct direction down a group.

modelAnswer: Across a period, atomic radius generally decreases from left to right.
Down a group, atomic radius generally increases.

items.followUp: Define a covalent bond and give one example.

rubric.why: An ionic bond is the attraction between oppositely charged ions, usually formed after electron transfer.
rubric.description: Defines an ionic bond as the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct definition identifying the oppositely charged ions and their attraction.

rubric.why: A correct ionic compound is needed as an example.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of an ionic compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example such as sodium chloride.

modelAnswer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic force of attraction between oppositely charged ions, formed when electrons are transferred from one atom to another.
Sodium chloride (NaCl) is an example of an ionic compound.
